If a curve $C$ is given by $y=\frac{x}{{e}^{3x}},$ calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=1.$

The slope at $x=1$ is

In this case, the expression for $y$ is a quotient $\frac{u(x)}{v(x)}$ with $u(x)=x$ and $v(x)={e}^{3x}.$ 

Therefore, we apply the quotient rule as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{'}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{'}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{(x)}^{'}\cdot {e}^{3x}-x\cdot {({e}^{3x})}^{'}}{{({e}^{3x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot {e}^{3x}-x\cdot 3{e}^{3x}}{{({e}^{3x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3x}(1-3x)}{{({e}^{3x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1-3x}{{e}^{3x}}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=1$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}\,(1) & =\frac{1-3(1)}{{e}^{3(1)}} \\  & =\frac{-2}{{e}^{3}} \\  & =-\frac{2}{{e}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line at $x=1$ is $-\frac{2}{{e}^{3}}.$

raw_question.:question/problem: If a curve $C$ is given by $y=\frac{\operatorname{cos}x}{1+\operatorname{sin}x},$ calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$
raw_question.:question/worked-solution:
In this case, the expression for $y$ is a quotient $\frac{u(x)}{v(x)}$ with $u(x)=\operatorname{cos}x$ and $v(x)=1+\operatorname{sin}x.$ 

Therefore, we apply the quotient rule as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{'}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{'}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(\operatorname{cos}x)^{'}\cdot (1+\operatorname{sin}x)-\operatorname{cos}x\cdot (1+\operatorname{sin}x)^{'}}{(1+\operatorname{sin}x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(-\operatorname{sin}x)(1+\operatorname{sin}x)-(\operatorname{cos}x)\operatorname{cos}x}{(1+\operatorname{sin}x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(-\operatorname{sin}x-{sin}^{2}x-{cos}^{2}x)}{(1+\operatorname{sin}x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(-\operatorname{sin}x-({sin}^{2}x+{cos}^{2}x))}{(1+\operatorname{sin}x)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 Since ${sin}^{2}x+{cos}^{2}x=1$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{(-\operatorname{sin}x-1)}{(1+\operatorname{sin}x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-(1+\operatorname{sin}x)}{(1+\operatorname{sin}x)^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{1+\operatorname{sin}x}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-\frac{1}{1+\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{2})} \\  & =-\frac{1}{1+1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $-\frac{1}{2}.$
